summary: Defines an additional Cryptographic Message Syntax content type, authenticated-enveloped-data, for use with authenticated encryption modes. It supports the same key management techniques as the existing enveloped-data type. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a locked box that also has a tamper seal. It keeps the contents secret and lets the receiver know nobody changed them on the way.

questions: what is cms authenticated enveloped data
how does cms authenticated encryption work

subtitle: A CMS wrapper that encrypts a message and proves nobody changed it, in a single pass, for any number of recipients.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) had no content type built for authenticated encryption modes, where one algorithm both encrypts the content and authenticates it.
tldr.mechanism: The authenticated-enveloped-data content type encrypts and authenticates the content with a random key, then encrypts that key separately for each recipient using the same key management options as enveloped-data. Extra attributes can be authenticated without being encrypted.
tldr.outcome: Receivers get confidentiality and integrity from one structure, and must verify integrity before releasing any plaintext. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3852.

today: RFC 5083 is a Proposed Standard from November 2007 that updates RFC 3852, and no later RFC obsoletes it. The AES-CCM and AES-GCM conventions for using it are in RFC 5084.

sections.title: Why Another Content Type
sections.content:
RFC 5083 adds a new content type to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), called authenticated-enveloped-data. It is meant for authenticated encryption modes, where an arbitrary content is both authenticated and encrypted. Some associated data, in the form of authenticated attributes, can be authenticated too.

All the key management techniques that the existing CMS enveloped-data content type supports also work here. The conventions for using the AES-CCM and AES-GCM algorithms with this content type live in a companion document, RFC 5084. Like other CMS content types, this one is described in ASN.1 and uses the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).
sections.plainLanguage: Older locked boxes only kept secrets. This new kind keeps secrets and also has a seal that shows if the contents were changed.

sections.title: How an Envelope Is Built
sections.content:
The content, of any type, plus one encrypted key per recipient forms a digital envelope for each recipient. The sender builds it in steps:

  1. Generate a content-authenticated-encryption key at random.
  2. Encrypt that key for each recipient.
  3. Collect each encrypted key and recipient details into a RecipientInfo value (defined in Section 6.2 of RFC 3852).
  4. Collect attributes that are authenticated but not encrypted.
  5. Authenticate those attributes and authenticate and encrypt the content with the key, adding padding where the algorithm needs it.
  6. Collect attributes that get neither authentication nor encryption.
  7. Assemble everything into an AuthEnvelopedData value.

To open the envelope, a recipient decrypts one of the encrypted keys, then uses the recovered key to decrypt and verify the content and the authenticated attributes. The recipient MUST verify integrity before releasing any information, especially plaintext. If verification fails, the receiver MUST destroy all of the plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: You lock your note with a random key, then make a copy of that key for each friend, each locked in a way only that friend can open. A friend opens the box only if the seal checks out.

sections.title: The AuthEnvelopedData Structure
sections.content:
The content type is identified by the object identifier id-ct-authEnvelopedData, which ends in 23, and its value MUST have the ASN.1 type AuthEnvelopedData. Its fields are:

  • version: the syntax version, which MUST be set to 0.
  • originatorInfo: optional, present only if the key management algorithm needs it. It may carry certificates and CRLs.
  • recipientInfos: per-recipient information, with at least one element.
  • authEncryptedContentInfo: the authenticated and encrypted content, using the same type that enveloped-data uses.
  • authAttrs: optional authenticated attributes. They MUST be present if the content type inside is not id-data, and MUST be DER encoded even if the rest is BER. The message-digest attribute SHOULD NOT be included.
  • mac: the integrity check value or message authentication code produced by the authenticated encryption algorithm. It covers the authenticated attributes and the content directly, so no separate digest algorithm is used.
  • unauthAttrs: optional attributes with no protection.

The RFC also explains version numbers: a higher number is assigned whenever the structure changes, but a sender uses the lowest version that supports the syntax it generates, for maximum interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope has labelled slots: who can open it, the locked message, notes that are sealed along with it, the seal itself, and notes written on the outside that anyone can read or change.

sections.title: Authenticate and Encrypt
sections.content:
The inputs to the authenticated encryption algorithm are the content (padded if needed), the DER-encoded authenticated attributes (padded if needed) and the random key. The attributes are called the additional authenticated data (AAD): they are authenticated but not encrypted. Padding, where required, follows Section 6.3 of RFC 3852, and that method is well defined only if the block size is less than 256 octets.

To build the AAD, the authAttrs field is encoded separately. The implicit [1] tag is not used for this encoding. Instead a universal SET OF tag is encoded, followed by the length and content octets of the attributes. If there are no authenticated attributes, zero bits of input are given for the AAD.

The encrypted data goes into encryptedContent as an OCTET STRING, and the authentication tag goes into the mac field.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender scrambles the message and stamps a seal that depends on both the message and the sealed notes. The scrambled message goes in one slot and the seal in another.

sections.title: Delivering the Key to Each Recipient
sections.content:
Only the value of the content-authenticated-encryption key is fed to the recipient's key-encryption algorithm. Any of four techniques can be used for each recipient of the same content, and different recipients can use different ones:

  • Key transport: the key is encrypted in the recipient's public key.
  • Key agreement: the recipient's public key and the sender's private key produce a pairwise symmetric key-encryption key, which encrypts the content key.
  • Symmetric key-encryption keys: the key is encrypted with a previously distributed symmetric key.
  • Passwords: the key is encrypted with a key derived from a password or other shared secret.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to hand a friend their copy of the key: lock it with their public padlock, make a secret together, use a code you already share, or use a password.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3852 apply here too. Many authenticated encryption algorithms use a block cipher in counter mode, which gives strong confidentiality when used properly. It is easy to misuse, though: if counter block values are ever used for more than one encryption with the same key, the same key stream encrypts both plaintexts and confidentiality is lost. This content type avoids that because every key management technique allows a fresh key for each content, and counter-mode algorithms support an unpredictable nonce, sometimes called a salt, carried in an algorithm identifier parameter.

Implementations must randomly generate keys, padding and nonces. Poor pseudo-random number generators can leave keys easy to reproduce, and the RFC points to RFC 4086 for guidance.

The message-digest attribute SHOULD NOT be included in the authenticated attributes, because it holds an unencrypted hash of the plaintext. Disclosing it enables content tracking and lets someone test whether the plaintext matches a candidate.

Encrypted messages hide their plaintext from the spam and phishing defenses that read message text. The RFC suggests software handle this, for example by rejecting or discarding encrypted messages unless they come from a member of a white list.
sections.plainLanguage: Never reuse a lock pattern: using the same scrambling pattern twice lets a snoop figure out both notes. Also do not write a fingerprint of the note on the outside, because people could use it to guess what is inside.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content: Section 4 gives the formal ASN.1 module, CMS-AuthEnvelopedData-2007, using implicit tags. It imports AuthAttributes, CMSVersion, EncryptedContentInfo, MessageAuthenticationCode, OriginatorInfo, RecipientInfos and UnauthAttributes from the CMS module of RFC 3852, and then defines the object identifier and the AuthEnvelopedData sequence. Nothing new beyond Section 2.1 is introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the exact blueprint that computers use so everyone builds the envelope the same way.

data.title: AuthEnvelopedData
data.code:
AuthEnvelopedData ::= SEQUENCE {
  version CMSVersion,
  originatorInfo [0] IMPLICIT OriginatorInfo OPTIONAL,
  recipientInfos RecipientInfos,
  authEncryptedContentInfo EncryptedContentInfo,
  authAttrs [1] IMPLICIT AuthAttributes OPTIONAL,
  mac MessageAuthenticationCode,
  unauthAttrs [2] IMPLICIT UnauthAttributes OPTIONAL }

items.title: Key transport
items.text: Content key encrypted in the recipient's public key.

items.title: Key agreement
items.text: Pairwise key from the recipient's public key and the sender's private key.

items.title: Symmetric KEK
items.text: Content key encrypted in a previously distributed symmetric key.

items.title: Password
items.text: Key-encryption key derived from a password or shared secret.
